steps.title: Why we lock data
text: Anyone can listen on a network wire. If you send a secret as readable bytes, the listener reads it too.
{{term:aes}} is a lock for data. It turns readable {{term:plaintext}} into scrambled {{term:ciphertext}}, and only the right {{term:key}} turns it back.
This lesson shows three ways to use AES. Two of them hide your data well, and one of them leaks patterns. You will see which.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

steps.title: Both sides hold the same key
text: The client and the server now hold one 16-byte key. The same key locks the data and unlocks it.
Look at the secrets panel. Both lanes list the key, because both sides need it.
Real programs agree on a key with a key exchange. Lesson 3 shows how that works.

steps.title: Readable in, scrambled out
text: This is the first message, locked with AES in {{term:gcm}} mode. At the moment the key went in, the readable blue bytes turned into scrambled amber ones.
Open the Message bytes panel. The cipher field holds the ciphertext. The {{term:nonce}} is a number used once, and the {{term:tag}} is a seal that catches changes.
Try it: switch to the eavesdropper view. You will see what a listener sees, which is a nonce, a tag, and noise.

steps.title: Blocks, chains, and the IV
text: AES works on {{term:block}}s of 16 bytes. A long message is cut into blocks, and each block is locked in turn.
{{term:cbc}} mode chains the blocks. Each block is mixed with the one before it, so a repeated block locks to different bytes.
The first block has nothing before it, so CBC starts with a random {{term:iv}}. Find the iv field in the Message bytes panel.

steps.title: ECB locks each block alone
text: {{term:ecb}} is the simplest mode. It locks every 16-byte block on its own, with no chain between blocks.
The trouble is that two equal blocks give two equal locked blocks. In a picture, big patches of one color repeat, so the pattern survives the lock.
Look at the locked picture in the Picture tab. The outline of the shape still shows through.

claims.text: ECB mode locks equal plaintext blocks to equal ciphertext blocks, so patterns in the data can show in the ciphertext.

steps.title: Count the leak
text: The server counted the repeated blocks in the locked picture. The count is a measured number from the trace, and the screen invents nothing.
A good lock gives a count near zero. ECB gives a large count, and that count is the leak.
Try it: send the text message in ECB as well. The result says that no check caught it, because the lock itself works and the mode is the weak part.

tryIt.label: Send the text message in ECB

steps.title: CBC and GCM hide the shape
text: Here is the same picture locked with GCM. It looks like noise, and the outline is gone.
CBC gives the same result. Check the repeat count on each picture: it stays near zero.

steps.title: GCM catches edits
text: Locking hides data. It leaves the bytes open to edits, so GCM adds a tag that catches edits.
The server checks the tag before it trusts a message. On the normal run, the check passed.
Try it: flip one bit of the locked text. The tag no longer fits, the check fails, and the server refuses the message.

tryIt.label: Flip one bit in the GCM text

claims.text: GCM decryption checks the authentication tag first and returns no plaintext when the tag check fails.

steps.title: A nonce must never repeat
text: GCM needs a fresh nonce for every message under one key. A repeat can let an attacker compare two messages and forge new ones.
Real GCM has no alarm for this mistake. The lab adds a detector so you can see it.
Try it: send the last message with the first nonce. The detector fails the check.

claims.text: GCM needs a nonce that is unique for each message under one key. A repeated nonce exposes the data and lets an attacker forge messages.
claims.source: NIST SP 800-38D, section 8 (Uniqueness Requirement on IVs and Keys) and Appendix A (if IVs repeat, an adversary will likely learn the hash subkey and can construct a forgery)

claims.text: The nonce reuse detector is a lab engine event. Real GCM has no built-in alarm for a repeated nonce.
claims.source: NIST SP 800-38D, Appendix A (in most cases the authenticated decryption function cannot detect an IV repetition); docs/ux-design.md, section 8, lesson 1 row (the detector is an engine event)

steps.title: Some edits slip through
text: Now flip one bit in the CBC message. No check fails, and that is the point of this step.
One block of the unlocked text turns to junk. The next block changes by that one bit, and an attacker can aim that change.
CBC hides data but cannot see edits. That is why modern designs pair a lock with a tag, as GCM does.

tryIt.label: Flip one bit in the CBC text

claims.text: In CBC, flipping one ciphertext bit garbles that block's plaintext and flips the same bit in the next block's plaintext.
claims.source: NIST SP 800-38A, section 6.2 (CBC mode); docs/lessons-1-3-names.md, Lesson 1 attacks, L1-flip-cbc

steps.title: What to take away
text: ECB hides the bytes but leaks patterns. CBC hides patterns but lets edits through. GCM hides patterns and catches edits.
Pick a mode that does both jobs, and give each message its own nonce.
